problems.title: Percentiles

parts.prompt: How many samples are above p99.9?

options: a strategy acts on every event; rare slow events cost money and cluster in volatile markets

problems.solution: 1,000 slow events per million is a lot of trades.

problems.title: Trace a book
hints: Trades are at the resting price.
problems.solution: 3 buys 4 from 1 at 100; 4 sells 6 to 1 at 100 (not 99); 4 lots of order 4 rest at 99.

problems.title: Cancel cost
problems.statement: A book with 10⁵ resting orders; cancels are 20× more frequent than trades.

parts.prompt: Why not find-and-erase in a heap?

options: lazy deletion with an id→order map
price levels with intrusive lists + id map
re-sort the book on every cancel

problems.solution: Lazy deletion is O(log n) amortised; intrusive lists give O(1) unlink.

problems.title: Price array
problems.statement: Prices lie within ±5,000 ticks of a reference.

parts.prompt: Array size for levels per side?

options: O(1) level access, contiguous memory, no tree rebalancing

problems.solution: Track the best index and scan forward when a level empties.

problems.title: Coordinated omission
problems.statement: A load generator sends the next request only after the previous reply. The server stalls for 1 s once during a 100 s test at 1,000 req/s.

parts.prompt: Requests that should have been sent during the stall?
Slow samples the naive tool records?

hints: The tool stops sending while waiting.
problems.solution: One bad sample instead of ~1,000, so the percentiles look far better than reality.

problems.title: Kernel bypass
problems.statement: Kernel UDP receive path ~6 µs; kernel-bypass ~1 µs; tick-to-trade budget 5 µs.

parts.prompt: Can the kernel path meet the budget?

problems.solution: That's why low-latency stacks bypass the kernel.

problems.title: Hot path hygiene
problems.statement: Which belong on a microsecond hot path?

options: binary records into an SPSC log ring

problems.title: Integer prices
problems.statement: Why are prices stored as integer ticks?

options: exact equality and ordering at price levels; 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in floating point
